segments.text: "If you do everything, you will win." That is the maxim by which Lyndon
Johnson lived his life. My guest today is Robert Caro.
Over the 50 years that he has spent writing about Lyndon Johnson, he has lived in the
edges of the Texas Hill Country to understand the poverty and loneliness of Johnson’s youth.
He has sifted through millions of documents in the Senate and presidential libraries
of the entire nation. He has chased down for
interviews everyone, from the former goon who helped Johnson steal an election to the chauffeur
who drove him on his first desperate campaign. In other words, my guest today is a man
who understands Johnson’s aphorism: "If you do everything, you’ll win."
Mr. Caro, it is such a huge honor to have you on the show.
It’s great to be here. My first question is what
I hinted at in the introduction. How much do you see yourself
represented in Johnson or in Moses? Is part of the reason you’re able to
write so compellingly about them that you share some of their qualities?
Let me say first, I think, I hope, there are qualities of both these guys that I don’t share.
Among other things they’re so, I’ll use the word, ruthless.
You say they’d do anything to win. That’s part of their greatness.
I remember when I started learning about Robert Moses, I went to the La Guardia
papers, which were kept in the Boat Basin. They were stored by the Municipal Archives,
literally in the 79th Street Boat Basin on the Hudson River, three levels down.
There was this row of file cabinets against the wall.
I’m sitting there day after day going through these documents.
Occasionally I’d come across a note that Robert Moses wrote, and I realized I’m
following the same path he was. It’s fascinating, actually.
Obviously, not all the qualities. But the quality I’m referring to
here is that just like Johnson or just like Moses, you refuse to take no for an answer.
If somebody says, "I won’t give you an interview," you don’t stop there.
You refuse to leave a stone unturned. So there is a relentlessness that
you share with these subjects. I’m going to take that as a compliment.
Yes. You feel there are certain people that you have to interview.
If they don’t want to give you an interview, you can’t, I feel, say no.
Like Lyndon Johnson’s first secretary, the one who rode in the car with him on the campaigns.
I said, "There’s no other human being on earth who knows what Lyndon Johnson is doing all
these hours driving back and forth across Texas. I don’t know what I have to do, but I have to get
him to tell me honestly about this thing." This raises another question
that I wanted to ask you. You’re interviewing all these people,
and in many cases, they must know that it’s not good for them to tell you what you want to know.
In many cases, they tell you anyway. How do you get people to tell you things
that they know they shouldn’t tell you? You ask terrific questions. Sometimes
you’re sitting there and you know this person doesn’t want to talk to you about what you
want to get out of them, like John Connally on how Johnson used money to get political power.
I’m thinking, "But I’ve been through the notes. Connally collected the money and gave it out at
Johnson’s instructions, so he’s the only guy who can tell me how Johnson did this,
how he judged who to give money to." Sometimes Johnson would write
on a request for money. If the guy asked for $1,500,
Johnson would write, "Okay, 1,500." Sometimes he’d write 500, sometimes he’d
write no, but sometimes he’d write, "No, never." I asked Connally what that meant, and he said,
"This guy was never going to get money from Lyndon Johnson."
Then when you ask why he felt this way about this particular congressman, that’s when the
really fascinating stories emerge. Before we get more into Johnson,
I want to first start with Moses. In the last decade or two,
people have been complaining that it’s become too hard and too difficult to build things,
especially for the government to build things. If you look at the Second Avenue subway,
they’ve been building it for around 50 years. They’ve opened up a mile and a half.
It cost more than $4 billion. People have been saying,
"The Power Broker came out. It was an immensely influential book.
We were concerned about so much power being centralized and delegated to one
person so they could build. We wanted to prevent that,
and so we made environmental review and land use review and community boards and litigation."
People say, "We’ve overcorrected. We’ve gone too far in the other direction."
What do you think of that? They also say that because
of all these safeguards, Robert Moses could not operate in the same way today.
But the fact is, when Robert Moses started, there were also safeguards.
People were also saying, "You can’t build anything."
This was in the 1920s. People were saying,
"Government can’t build anything. There are too many blocks.
Nothing’s getting built. We need highways. It’s the age of cars.
Everyone’s getting automobiles, but we have the same old roads.
Nobody can build them because the property owners don’t want the roads built through their land."
Robert Moses comes along, and all of a sudden those things vanish because, despite all the
safeguards and everything else, he just builds. Doing The Power Broker, it was just fascinating
to me to see how he gets around everything. It doesn’t matter what it is.
He’s going to build a beach at Jones Beach. He sees it one day.
He says, "This is the greatest beach I’ve ever seen.
It’s only 27 miles from New York City. If I can build a road out here, I will give
the people of New York City this great beach." But it seems impossible to build that road
because the property owners don’t want the road going through their farms and property.
He basically says, "I’m going to build it." To watch him do it, to overcome each obstacle,
there are so many, and then all of a sudden it’s open and you have Jones
Beach and you have it accessible to New York. It’s an act of political genius, and it’s also
an act of will: "I’m going to do it." That’s fascinating to learn about.
So you think today if there were a Moses-type figure, they would figure out a way to work
around everything that’s been set up? The answer to that is, when Moses was
building, they were saying the same thing. "Nobody’s ever going to build.
We need roads for the automobiles, but they’d have to go through
dozens of farms, scores of properties. No one’s ever going to be able to do it."
But he comes along and does it. So today someone would come along and do it.
This, I think, is a profound question for democracies: how do we end up in a
place which is not the extremes of ’50s or ’60s Moses, but also not where we are now?
Where I live in California, we’ve spent, I don’t know, $15 billion over the last decade.
We haven’t gotten a single new line or single new mile of railway that
those $15 billion have been spent to build. Whereas in a different system… You could say China
today is like New York City in the ’40s and ’50s. They have a very Moses-type attitude and they
put up tens of thousands of miles of railways over the last 10-20 years.
But of course, at the cost of similar amounts of displacement of people and recklessness.
So how do we land in a good spot between either extreme?
I’m not sure there is a good spot. What you just said is the situation.
To build anything on a large scale, you’re confronted with dozens or
scores or perhaps hundreds of property owners who don’t want it built there.
So the question is, how does anything get built? Then someone comes along and can do it.
When Robert Moses started, it seemed impossible, actually impossible, to build roads out into
Long Island because the road would have to cross scores of properties, most of whose
owners didn’t want the roads coming through. They had the power to stop them then because
he didn’t have the power of eminent domain. But Moses said basically, "I’m going to build it."
He would find a way to overcome each difficulty. What am I trying to say by that?
I’m trying to say that every once in a while someone comes along who’s a genius,
if that’s the right word, at getting big things built for the public.
Decades may pass when there’s no one like that. You say, "Everything’s stalled. Nothing big
is ever going to be built again." Then someone suddenly comes along
and all of a sudden things get built. That’s the nature of political genius.
I happen to be writing about two guys, Lyndon Johnson and Robert Moses, Johnson with civil
rights and Moses with public works, where people were saying, "You can’t do this."
But they did it. Correct me if I’m putting
words in your mouth, but if I may attempt an interpretation of what you said, it sounds like
you think we need a little Moses today. A great insight. I sometimes wonder
about just what you said. The answer is, I certainly
don’t want someone who’s as ruthless and disregarding public opinion as a Robert Moses.
But at the same time, you need someone who’s going to find a way to get things built.
He’s going to have to find a way despite the fact that so many people don’t want it built.
A lot of people who haven’t read the book have this impression that you think everything
Moses did was bad, and that we need to make sure that we can never have a Moses again.
So it’s interesting to hear you say that we need a little Moses again.
When people say to me everything was bad that he did, what I say is, "You didn’t read the book."
Because certainly the first parts of the book, hundreds of pages, are about a young idealist
who sees this great need for recreation, for beaches on Long Island for the city people,
and is going to find a way to make them accessible to people in the city.
It’s an act of genius and willpower the way he does it, and that’s great.
Now, does it evolve into where Moses listens to nobody, and the only thing that matters is
what he wants to get built? It does evolve into that.
He does change. But the young Moses, the idealist, before he’s building, is an expert
in the technicalities of civil service. He devotes all his energies to trying to
reform the civil service so that people get promoted on merit instead of political pull.
He works so hard at that. You see a real idealism.
You see a real idealism in his early works, when he says, "I want to make
these beaches accessible to New York." Now, does that evolve into "I think there
ought to be a highway here no matter what anybody says, and no matter how
many thousands of people are in the way," like the Cross Bronx Expressway, "I’ll evict them"?
It does. He changes. That to me is a big part of the story of The Power Broker:
how this guy who’s in the beginning a young, idealistic guy who wants to build to make
lives better for people, to give them access to the ocean and beaches, changes into someone who
just wants to build because he thinks something should be built no matter what anyone else says.
He’s going to do it no matter how many hundreds, thousands of people he has to evict,
no matter how bad an idea it is, like the Cross Bronx Expressway.
People are telling him not to do that before he does it.
The minute this road opens, it’s the world’s longest traffic jam.
Not thousands, but tens of thousands of people were evicted, thrown out of their
homes by him without any relocation provisions. So in a way it’s a story of how you give somebody
power without the power, in a way — I don’t want to use the word "corrupting" him — but hardening
him to anyone who opposes him, to any opposition. Coding agents work best when they get fast,
detailed feedback. My sponsor, Antithesis,
gives your agents some of the richest feedback there is by running every change they make
through thousands of hostile simulations. This usually isn't feasible. Simulation
testing is hard. It normally requires rebuilding your software around a fake network and clock,
among other things. So most teams don't bother.
Even if they do, getting enough coverage typically takes hours.
So they run these simulations overnight, by which point all the day's changes are jumbled together,
and it's harder for the agents to tell which PR broke something.
Antithesis solves both problems. It runs your software inside a fully
deterministic simulated computer, so you don't have to rebuild anything yourself.
And it explores fast enough that you can test every PR.
On a recent project, it packed 15 hours of simulation testing into each 15-minute run.
That speed comes from both parallelism and branching.
Because it's deterministic, whenever Antithesis finds an interesting state,
it can save that exact moment and branch off hundreds of different futures.
It never wastes time replaying events, hoping to stumble across that state again.
And it doesn't just explore randomly.
Antithesis systematically injects faults and tweaks your system in
the ways most likely to break it. So every minute in Antithesis is
one of the unluckiest hours your software will ever experience.
Learn more at antithesis.com/dwarkesh. You start writing the book in ’66, ’67.
You’re writing it while Moses is losing power. His career is not over yet.
So the story changes while you’re writing it. I don’t know if you’ve talked about that,
but presumably the conclusion changes because you don’t know whether he’s
going to lose that power or not when you start. That’s a great question. I watch that happen,
and I’m young. Whatever my age was,
I didn’t really know what I was doing. I watched him lose power, and I learned enough
about him to know how sad this was going to be. If I could think a moment, there's a moment that
this happened… Yeah… His office was still up at the Triborough Bridge Authority.
When he was in power, I interviewed him in that office several times.
You felt his power. You felt outside there were all these people sitting
around waiting for his decisions. As soon as I finished, the secretary
would come in with a list of telephone calls from people who had called wanting
something from him while I was talking to him. I remember I had one long interview with him.
Maybe it was my last one. By the time I finished, I realized
there had been no calls. The secretary had nothing to tell him.
So whatever you thought of Moses, you felt the poignance of someone losing power.
That’s fascinating. That’s what I was wondering about.
You couldn’t help feeling sad for him, even though you knew what he had done.
You couldn’t help feeling, "Oh, this is, in a way, tragic that no one’s calling
and asking him for a favor anymore." Did he realize that was happening?
I don’t think he really did. In a way, I’m sure he did.
But by that time he was so insulated. Whatever his age was, he was up in his 80s.
He was deaf. He still had at the Triborough headquarters on Randall’s Island all these
Moses men who were loyal to him and treated him with the same deference they always had.
He knew he wasn’t getting his projects done. But I know he felt he was just going to keep
pushing like he always did, and he was going to win again.
The answer to your question is no, I don’t think he did ever realize that.
In, I think, ’62, as you say, he tries to pull a trick on Nelson Rockefeller that he had pulled on
countless previous mayors and governors, which is to threaten to resign if he didn’t get his way.
Rockefeller says, "I regretfully accept," and nothing happens.
That made me wonder as I was reading it. Could all those previous governors and mayors who
were getting threatened have done the same thing? Great question. Yeah, the answer is yes.
Well, you say, "could they have done the same thing?"
In part, the answer is yes. They had the power to fire him.
He wasn’t an elected official. But there wasn’t really a possibility.
The answer to the question at the bottom is no, they couldn’t, because he was simply too popular.
You couldn’t fire Robert Moses. That’s like firing some person
who was the idol of New York. But in addition, with his genius,
he had created, in all his different posts — chairman of the State Power Authority,
chairman of Triborough Bridge Authority, Parks Commissioner, Long Island Parks Commissioner,
Jones Beach Commissioner — such an interlocking web that you couldn’t fire him from everything,
because the terms ended in different ways, and some you didn’t have the power to fire him from.
He had really made it impossible. Well, almost impossible, because at the end,
if you wanted to do it, Rockefeller did it. But by that time,
cracks had appeared in the armor. I think for decades, the answer to your
question is you couldn’t do it. But then as he got older,
cracks appeared in the armor. If you wanted to brave criticism
in all the newspapers and public criticism and everything else, you probably could have done it.
Which leads into the next question I want to ask you.
You interviewed him seven times. The seventh time, you mentioned
your awareness of a donation that was made to his commission by a millionaire whose golf course was
spared by the new route for his parkway. After that, he didn’t talk to you again.
If you had gotten an eighth interview with Robert Moses, what is the one question
you would most want to ask him? Oh, God, what a great question.
Off the top of my head, if I only had one question to ask him, I’d ask him,
"Did you realize you were changing?" That’s off the top... That’s
a great question you asked. But that’s the answer I’ll give for now.
That’s something I always would like to have asked him.
Do you think he realized that he was changing? No. I think he felt from the beginning that he had
this vision to build roads here and parks there. That was the best thing to do.
It was going to get done, and it should get done. No matter how many hardships he had to inflict
on people, no matter how many thousands he had to evict, no matter what he had to do,
he was going to get the roads built. You see this increasing ruthlessness,
this utter ruthlessness of him. If someone stood in his way, he was going to
find a way to remove that person as an obstacle. I’ll give you an example of that if you want.
There’s a politician in the Bronx named Henry Epstein.
Henry Epstein is opposing the Cross Bronx Expressway.
He’s saying to Robert Moses, "You’re putting it right through a neighborhood where you
have to evict tens of thousands of people. You can just move it two blocks to the south,
and you only have to evict a couple of hundred people."
Moses sets out to destroy Epstein, and basically does, by making it known he’s having an affair.
If he can find a weakness in somebody, that he has a mistress,
that he’s taking money or something, he’ll use it. He’ll use whatever he has to to get things done.
He learns that, in my opinion, by failing to get things done when he’s very young.
He has things that he wants to get done, and they don’t get done.
The awareness comes on him. We can see it in the book,
or in my learning about him. I try to show how he learns
that he has to find weaknesses in people. If he has a weakness, he’s going to use it.
He’s going to get things done. There’s a hardening, an increased
ruthlessness, where the only thing that matters is to get the thing done.
Anyone who stands in his way is going to get whatever it takes.
If Moses has to destroy him, he’ll destroy him. As you say, you’re writing not the history
of one man, but of an era in America. One of the most interesting things about
The Power Broker is, especially in the period in which he’s able to accomplish so much so quickly,
what’s happening, and you talk about this, is the Great Depression.
He’s hiring thousands of architects, tens of thousands of linemen, for pennies on the
dollar to do big public works for the city. So I wonder how big a part of Moses’ early
achievements is just that the government, because of the Great Depression, could
compete with the private sector for the top talent and for lots and lots of labor working
24/7 through the winter, moving fast. Another great question. The answer is
that it played a big role. He needed architects for something.
I don’t remember what it is. It’s in The Power Broker.
They lined up on Fifth Avenue, thousands of out-of-work architects
that he could hire for very low wages. But more than the wages, they were available,
because they didn’t have anything to do. He was able to hire so many people,
and hire and fire them in a ruthless way, making the workmen work hard.
He could just fire them. It was the Depression. They
didn’t have other jobs to go to. He used that. Yes.
As somebody who has studied urban development so deeply, here is one thing I’m curious about.
You look at the things that were built at the beginning of the last century,
or before the beginning of the last century — Grand Central Station and all the beautiful
architecture in New York — versus the things that were built in the second half of the century.
They look a lot less beautiful. The earlier, more beautiful things
were built by a much poorer country. What changed? Why were you able to
build more beautiful things before? One thing that changed is you had all
these out-of-work artisans who could, we’ll just say, carve stonework on buildings.
My apartment is on the 15th floor of an apartment house.
Across the street is a building that’s 15-16 stories high.
You say, "Look at all the beautiful carving that’s done in the stonework
of that building up on the roof." I said, "The only people who can
see it are the people in my apartment and the people in the apartment next to it."
Someone was willing to spend that money because the builders who built that could
hire skilled people at such low wages that they could make them do the decorations
to make a building beautiful up on floors that nobody’s going to see, because people came cheap.
If you want your agents to do real work, they need to be able to use
the tools that your company runs on. Things like email or Slack or Stripe.
But giving them unfettered access is risky, because they could send
confidential information to a customer or refund a bunch of payments that they shouldn't have.
Of course, you could just review every request manually, but that doesn't typically last.
That's why my sponsor, WorkOS, built Airlock. It's a judgment layer that sits between
your agents and your tools. Any time that an agent wants to
do something, it makes a request to Airlock, which evaluates it against
your company's policies and decides whether to allow it, block it, or escalate it to a human.
Whenever a request is allowed, Airlock takes the relevant action for the agent,
hitting the necessary endpoints and passing along the response.
That way, your agents never see your API keys, and so they can't leak them
or use them for unauthorized purposes. Since Airlock holds the keys to all your
tools, it has to be rock solid. Fortunately, WorkOS has spent the
better part of the last decade building auth and permissions products, and they're battle-tested.
More than 3,000 companies rely on WorkOS, including OpenAI and Anthropic.
Airlock is in early access. If you're interested, go to workos.com/airlock.
I want to ask you about Johnson now. In Master of the Senate, you make two
points about how Johnson is effective, at least this is the way I read it.
One is that he’s very persuasive if you’re talking to him.
The other is he’s put himself in a position of leverage such that he has things to
promise you or things to threaten you with. It’s not that he’s convinced you of anything,
but you know that you need his favor if you want to be successful.
Of the two, I’m curious which was really the source of his power:
his leverage or his persuasion? Behind his persuasion was the power.
When you were talking to him, if he asked something of you,
you knew he had the power behind him to give you or deny you things that you wanted.
Say he was asking a senator for a vote on a specific issue.
The senator might not agree with him, might not want to give him the vote, but he would know.
He wants a committee assignment. Johnson has the power to give him that or not.
Or he would know he wants a specific law. Johnson has the power to get
that law passed or not. Behind everything — when Johnson
is talking to you, and he puts his arm around you, and he leans into you — it’s not just the force of
his personality that he’s bringing to bear on you. Behind that personality, you know he has the
power to do things to you or for you that you better be aware of.
Means of Ascent, the book about the election with Coke Stevenson, the 1948 Senate election.
That is my favorite book perhaps ever. You paint such a compelling portrait of this
person, Coke Stevenson, governor of Texas. They called him Mr. Texas.
As you were writing his profile and writing this book, did part of you wish
that he had won the Senate election? You couldn’t help feeling… I’ll
answer you directly. The answer is yes. I
think Coke Stevenson, although he was an idealist, he knew how to get things done.
When he was governor of Texas, he really accomplished things.
I think if he had gone to the Senate, he would have been a great senator and accomplished things.
So you wish that he had won. You feel the tragedy that
he lost because of the way he lost. The thing about Coke Stevenson, he really
didn’t realize someone could do all the things to him in the election that Lyndon Johnson did.
He didn’t come to grips with that. Suppose that Kennedy wins in ’60,
but Johnson refuses the vice presidency, so he’s still majority leader.
How different do you think the bills that Kennedy would pass under Johnson as majority
leader would be from the laws that Johnson as president was eventually able to pass?
That is to say, the things that happened in ’63 and ’64 and ’65,
would they have just happened earlier? No, because Kennedy did not have the
overriding desire to change America. John Kennedy was utterly charming.
He was a good president. He was good in foreign policy,
where Johnson certainly was not. But what he did not have was this
vision, this desire to change America that Lyndon Johnson had.
Lyndon Johnson comes back from his year teaching the poor kids in Cotulla determined to change the
education system to help poor people more, to do all these other things to help poor people.
That determination is something that’s really unique.
It’s what made him domestically such a great president, that we have all these
civil rights laws, these anti-poverty laws that we wouldn’t have had without Lyndon Johnson.
His presidency ends in tragedy because of foreign policy, because of Vietnam.
But he has this desire to get things done to help people in America that’s almost unique.
You say, "Gee, he’s determined to do this." He’s going to find a way to do it.
You watch him doing it. Then you say, "He was doing it."
When his attention turns to Vietnam, everything falls apart, and his presidency is ruined.
The things he started out to do domestically don’t get done in the way he would have done them.
But he starts out after the election with the education laws, with the anti-poverty
bills to change the country. He’s on his way to doing it.
That’s the great tragedy of Johnson and Vietnam. If I can ask about that, and it’s okay if you
don’t want to talk about this because it’s in the next book.
But if you’re willing to talk about it, fundamentally,
why did Johnson keep escalating, even when— The answer to your question is I’m still trying
to figure that out right now, so I’m not going to— That’s fine.
Because that’s quite a mystery. One of the things that’s true of
both Johnson and Moses is this inexhaustible energy, working 16
hours a day, sometimes even more than that. I wonder how much you think that is the fact
that they had a different constitution, that they just had different reserves of energy.
Or do you think it was just that their will was so strong?
I think it’s just their will. A lot of people have their energy.
When you see Robert Moses sleeping very little, showing that he’d do anything to get his way,
to get things done, being tired or something doesn’t even seem to figure into the equation.
Sometimes I’m looking at something — I can’t remember one off the top of
my head — and you’ll say, "Johnson’s making this call at 2:00 and 3:00 in the morning.
He’s up making these calls to get his way." In fact, there’s a funny anecdote.
Johnson calls one senator at 5:00 AM to ask him for his vote on something,
and the senator says, "Oh, Lyndon, I was just lying here waiting for your call."
So it’s their will. I want to ask you a little bit about writing biography now.
One question I have is, you spend 5-10 years writing a single book.
Through that process, maybe your editor and your wife are
the only people who have seen the manuscript. So how do you make sure you’re on the right track?
Because you’ve got to wait so long from when you start to when you get public feedback.
How do you make sure that everything’s going to hang together and you’re
pursuing the message the way you want to? Part of your question is, how do you be
sure you’re on the right track? The answer to that is you’re not.
But how do you try to stay on the right track? I do have a device for that.
Before I start a book — I learned this the hard way with The Power Broker, because I didn’t do
it with The Power Broker — I think through what I want the book to be, the whole book.
People say, "You mean you think it through to the end?"
The answer is yes. Then you say, "What is this book about?"
I sit at that desk sometimes for a long time before I start writing, when I’m
thinking about the book, just asking myself in one way or another, "What is this book about?"
You’ve got to get it down to one sentence. You say, "You can’t get it down to one sentence."
Then you say, "Yeah, but Bob, you learned you better get it down to one sentence,
or three years from now you’re going to be writing and you’re going to be saying, ‘What am I trying
to do?’" Before I start a book, I try to get it down to a sentence or at most a paragraph and say,
"Really, what is this book about?" I try to make everything
hang together around that point. Back in August, my sponsor, Jane Street, released

metal layers fit together to actually comprise the logic of the chip, and then showed each component
of our puzzle design, what it does, and how they reverse-engineered it, before then showing how
it all fits back together into the puzzle. Don't worry if you missed this challenge.
